# Piyajātika Sutta (MN 87 (PTS MN ii 106))
**ID:** MN 87 (PTS MN ii 106)
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Piyajātika Sutta
**Title (English, from literature):** Born From the Beloved
**PTS:** MN ii 106
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/mn87
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0202m.mul3.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Piyajātika Sutta* ("Born From the Beloved", MN 87; PTS MN ii 106) is the eighty-seventh discourse of the Majjhimanikāya, located in the *Rājavagga* ("Section on Kings") [Galasek 2016]. It is the first of four consecutive suttas in the collection (MN 87–90) featuring King Pasenadi of Kosala [Batchelor 2015]. Set in Jeta's Grove near Sāvatthi, the narrative begins when a grieving householder, devastated by the death of his only son, approaches the Buddha [Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995]. The Buddha informs him that sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are born from and rooted in what is beloved (*piyajātika*) [Galasek 2016; Ngoc Cuong Le 2018]. When the householder and a gathering of gamblers dismiss this teaching, news of the controversy reaches the Kosalan court [SuttaCentral; Galasek 2016]. King Pasenadi initially rejects the assertion, but Queen Mallikā dispatches the brahman Nāḷijaṅgha to the Buddha to confirm the exact teaching, subsequently guiding the king to insight through a method of cross-questioning regarding his grief should harm befall those he holds dear [SuttaCentral; Blum 2013; Ngoc Cuong Le 2018].
Curated parallels in Chinese Āgama literature include Madhyama-āgama 216 (MĀ 216), Ekottara-āgama 13.3 (EĀ 13.3), and two individual translations: Taishō 91 (*Boluomen zi mingzhong ainian buli jing*) and Taishō 154.15 [SuttaCentral; Mei Ching Hsuan 2009]. DharmaNexus independently confirms alignments with the Chinese versions in the *Madhyama-āgama* (T 26), the *Ekottara-āgama* (T 125), and T 91, in addition to shared segments with Sanskrit fragments of the *Rāṣṭrapālasūtra* [DharmaNexus]. Within the Pāli canon, the sutta is referenced in the *Attadaṇḍasuttaniddesa* (Mnd 15) [SuttaCentral], with which DharmaNexus records extensive text reuse (over 7,000 characters, notably matching §15–21 of MN 87) [DharmaNexus]. Strong phraseological reuse is also identified with the *Raṭṭhapāla Sutta* (MN 82), the *Gāmaṇi Saṁyutta* (SN 42), and various sections of the *Aṅguttaranikāya* [DharmaNexus].
It also forms part of the traditional Sri Lankan examination curriculum for the *Prācīna Madhyama* grade [ICTS 2017].
